name: git log
shortDescription: Show commit logs. Browse the chronological history of commits, with powerful filtering and formatting options.
detailedDescription:
The `git log` command displays the commit history of the repository. Each entry shows the commit hash, author, date, and message. By default it shows all commits reachable from the current HEAD, from newest to oldest.

The real power of `git log` is in its formatting and filtering options. You can display a compact one-line-per-commit view, draw ASCII branch graphs, filter by author or date range, search commit messages, and follow the history of a specific file — even across renames.

For everyday use, most developers set up an alias like `git lg` that combines `--oneline`, `--graph`, and `--decorate` for a beautiful, compact history view.

parameters.description: Show each commit on a single line: abbreviated hash + first line of message. Essential for scanning history quickly.
Draw a text-based graph of branch and merge history alongside the log. Best combined with --oneline.
Show commits from all branches, not just the current one.
Show ref names (branch names, tags) next to commits.
parameters.default: Enabled by default in recent Git

parameters.description: Limit output to the last N commits.
Filter commits by author name or email. Supports partial matches.
Show commits after a specific date. Accepts formats like '2024-01-01', '2 weeks ago', 'yesterday'.
Filter commits whose messages match the given pattern.
Show the diff (patch) introduced by each commit. Combines log and diff.
Show file change statistics (insertions/deletions) for each commit.
Only show commits that modified the specified file or directory.
Follow file history across renames. Use with a single file path.

examples.title: Beautiful compact history (create an alias!)
examples.description: The most popular Git log format among developers. Set it up once and use it forever.
examples.code:
git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate

# Set up as an alias:
git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --all --decorate"

# Now just use:
git lg

examples.title: Find commits by a specific author
examples.description: See what a specific team member has committed.
examples.code:
git log --author="John" --oneline

# Combine with date range:
git log --author="John" --since="2024-01-01" --until="2024-06-30"

examples.title: Search commit messages
examples.description: Find commits that mention a specific feature, bug number, or keyword.
examples.code:
git log --grep="fix" --oneline
git log --grep="JIRA-1234" --oneline

# Case-insensitive search:
git log --grep="login" -i --oneline

examples.title: History of a specific file
examples.description: Track all changes made to a file, including across renames.
examples.code:
git log --follow -- src/auth/login.js

# With diffs:
git log --follow -p -- src/auth/login.js

examples.title: Show only the last 5 commits with stats
examples.code:
git log -5 --stat

# Output shows which files changed and how many
# lines were added/removed in each commit

commonMistakes.text: Without `--all`, `git log` only shows commits reachable from the current branch. Commits on other branches are hidden. Always use `--all` when you want a complete picture.
Set up the alias: `git config --global alias.lg 'log --oneline --graph --all --decorate -20'`. This gives you a beautiful, compact view of the last 20 commits across all branches.
In large repos, `git log` without `-n` can output thousands of commits. Always limit with `-n <count>` or pipe to a pager.
